newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians keep up protests but no payout seen.
newsitem.headline: Albanians keep up protests but no payout seen.

text.p: Thousands of Albanians protested for a 13th day on Monday to demand the right-wing government pay compensation after the collapse of popular but fraudulent investment schemes.
About 5,000 people marched in the Adriatic port of Vlore in the afternoon, whistling, clapping and calling for Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and his government to resign.
In a new twist, they sang regional songs but changed the words to ridicule ministers and accuse the government of taking their money.
Vlore students threatened to go on a hunger strike if the protesters' demands for compensation were not met.
"If by February 20 the people's demands are not met, the student leaders of Vlore university will go on hunger strike," they said in a petition to the authorities.
In a reference to the date when the statue of communist dictator Enver Hoxha was toppled six years ago in Tirana, they added: "February 20 toppled dictatorships".

Protests and riots have swept Albania for the past month since five popular get-rich-quick investment schemes collapsed, posing the most serious challenge to the pro-market government since it came to power in 1992.
In Vlore, representatives of political parties, including the ruling Democrats, anti-communist dissidents and protesters signed a charter demanding the government quit and hold general elections.
Vlore mayor Gezim Zile, a member of the ruling Democrats, told the crowd from a balcony that he supported their demands.
"You cannot force resignation as a condition on me because I love Vlore like you and if I resign Vlore will become a mess. I am with you and support your strike," Zile told the crowd.
Protests have been calmer in Vlore and Fier, to the north, since authorities withdrew riot police over the weekend and let the marches proceed.
But police in the capital Tirana have kept a close eye out for anyone trying to start a demonstration and they have broken up any gatherings quickly.
In Vlore, which has been the centre of protests, the National Commercial Bank opened for the first time in 10 days to distribute some of the frozen assets of the failed pyramid schemes.
About 50 people lined up outside the bank. One older woman showed a deposit certificate for 40,000 leks (about $400) and said she would receive 52 percent of that.
"It's better than nothing," she told reporters.

The government seized about $300 million in assets from two failed schemes last month and said it would distribute the money to clients, but the government has refused to pay any compensation from state coffers.
Attention is now focused on four other funds, which insist they are genuine business concerns, but have frozen customers' capital and cut interest payments sharply.

In Tirana, Vehbi Alimucaj, head of the biggest investment holding firm, Vefa, said angry investors should "roll up their sleeves and get back to work" instead of protesting and burning down buildings.
Vefa, a household name in Albania, froze the deposits of its 80,000 investors after the five fraudulent pyramid schemes went bust last month and caused a panic.
Alimucaj told Reuters in an interview that his investors had nothing to fear and would get back their deposits in three or four months after a climate of insecurity had passed.
"We are prepared and proceeding with a definite timetable for paying this capital," he said. Meanwhile, Vefa had cash and was making interest payments to 2,000 to 3,000 people a day.
